questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.syllabus_ref: A1.2 Data representation and computer logic (binary representation of integers; two's complement; overflow)
questions.subtopic: A1.2 Overflow in a two's-complement subtraction used as a comparison
questions.challenge_mechanism: A comparison written as a subtraction looks like arithmetic and is in fact a range question. The subtraction $a - b$ is performed in eight bits whether or not the true difference fits, and it silently wraps whenever $|a - b| > 127$. The failure is not random and not rare: exactly a quarter of all ordered pairs of representable values give the wrong answer, and the program gives no indication that anything went wrong.
questions.question:
An environmental control system stores each temperature reading as an eight-bit signed
integer in two's complement form, so the representable range is $-128$ to $127$. The system
compares two readings, $a$ and $b$, using the single line

```
if a - b < 0 then output "a is the lower reading"
```

and the subtraction is performed in eight bits, with no overflow detection.

(a) Explain what happens when the line is executed with $a = 100$ and $b = -50$, and state the
value the system compares with zero. \tag{3}

(b) Determine the range of values of the true difference $d = a - b$ for which the comparison
gives the correct result. \tag{4}

(c) Determine the number of ordered pairs $(a, b)$, with $a$ and $b$ each in the range
$-128$ to $127$, for which the comparison gives the wrong result, and hence the proportion of
all pairs that fail. \tag{5}

(d) State a comparison that is correct for every pair in the range, and justify it. \tag{4}

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what happens when the line is executed with $a = 100$ and $b = -50$, and state the value compared with zero.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the range of values of the true difference $d = a - b$ for which the comparison gives the correct result.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the number of ordered pairs $(a, b)$ in the range $-128$ to $127$ for which the comparison gives the wrong result, and hence the proportion that fail.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State a comparison that is correct for every pair in the range, and justify it.

questions.answer:
(a) The true difference is $100 - (-50) = 150$ (A1). Eight-bit two's complement can only
represent $-128$ to $127$, so $150$ cannot be stored; the value wraps by subtracting $256$ and
the system obtains $150 - 256 = -106$ (M1). Since $-106 < 0$ the system reports that
$a$ is the lower reading, which is wrong: $100 > -50$ (A1).

The general rule is that a result outside the representable range has $256$ added to or
subtracted from it until it falls inside, which is exactly what modular arithmetic does. No
flag is raised and no exception is thrown, so the error is invisible at run time.

(b) The comparison is correct exactly when the subtraction does not overflow, that is when the
true difference is itself representable (M1):

$$-128 \le a - b \le 127 \tag{A1}$$

Equivalently $-128 \le d \le 127$ (A1). Outside that interval the stored value differs from the
true difference by a multiple of $256$ and, because the magnitude of the correction is larger
than the magnitude of the value being represented, the sign is reversed (A1). For example
$d = 150$ is stored as $-106$, and $d = -150$ is stored as $+106$; in both cases the sign is
wrong and so is the comparison.

(c) For a given difference $d$, the number of ordered pairs with $a - b = d$ and both values
in $[-128, 127]$ is $256 - |d|$, valid for $-255 \le d \le 255$ (M1). Summing over the correct
range from part (b),

$$N_{\text{correct}} = \sum_{d=-128}^{127} (256 - |d|) = 24512 + 256 + 24384 = 49152 \tag{A1}$$

The total number of ordered pairs is (A1)

$$N_{\text{total}} = 256 + \sum_{d=-255}^{255} (256 - |d|) - 256 = \sum_{d=-255}^{255}(256-|d|) = 65536$$

so the number that fail is (A1)

$$N_{\text{wrong}} = 65536 - 49152 = 16384 \tag{A1}$$

and the proportion is $\dfrac{16384}{65536} = 0.25$: exactly one quarter of all comparisons
give the wrong answer.

(d) Compare the signs first, and subtract only when the signs match (M1):

```
if (a < 0) and (b >= 0) then output "a is the lower reading"
else if (a >= 0) and (b < 0) then output "a is the higher reading"
else if a - b < 0 then output "a is the lower reading"
else output "a is the higher reading"
```

Justification (A1): if the signs differ, the comparison is settled by the signs alone and no
subtraction is needed, which is precisely the case in which the true difference is largest and
the subtraction most likely to overflow. If both values are non-negative then
$a - b$ lies between $-127$ and $127$; if both are negative then $a - b$ also lies between
$-127$ and $127$ (A1). In either case the result is representable, so the subtraction cannot
overflow and the test is safe (A1).

An alternative correct answer is to widen the stored type before subtracting — for example by
promoting both operands to sixteen bits — since the difference of two eight-bit values always
fits in nine bits. This is simpler but costs memory in a system that stores thousands of
readings, which is why the sign test is preferred here.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (A1) for the true difference $150$. (M1) for the wrap-around, which must be explained
as a modular reduction rather than merely asserted. (A1) for $-106$ and the conclusion that the
output is wrong.

(b) (M1) for linking correctness to the absence of overflow. (A1) for the interval
$-128 \le d \le 127$. (A1) for restating it in terms of $d$. (A1) for noting that the sign is
reversed outside the interval — a candidate who gives the interval alone has not explained why
the comparison then fails.

(c) (M1) for $256 - |d|$ as the count for a given difference. (A1) for $49152$ correct pairs.
(A1) for $65536$ total pairs. (A1) for $16384$ failing pairs. (A1) for the proportion $0.25$.
Credit any correct route to the count, including a direct enumeration argument, but the
summation must be shown rather than asserted. Condone small arithmetic slips in the partial
sums if the method is sound and the final proportion is consistent with them.

(d) (M1) for a comparison that avoids the subtraction when the signs differ. (A1) for the
justification in terms of the signs. (A1) for the bound $|a - b| \le 127$ when the signs match.
(A1) for concluding that no overflow is then possible.

Accept the alternative of promoting to a wider type, with full marks, provided the candidate
states that nine bits suffice. Do not accept "check the sign of the result", which does not
work: after the wrap the sign of the stored value is a valid sign, just the wrong one.
questions.explanation:
The bug is a classic and it survives code review, because the line reads like arithmetic
and the arithmetic is correct. The problem is that it is not arithmetic — it is a range
question wearing arithmetic's clothes. The subtraction has to produce a result in eight bits,
and the result of a subtraction of two eight-bit values needs nine.

The reason the failure rate is exactly a quarter is worth seeing rather than taking on trust.
For any particular difference $d$, the number of ordered pairs that produce it is
$256 - |d|$, because the larger the difference the fewer starting values leave room for it.
Summing that over the representable differences gives $49152$ of the $65536$ possible pairs,
and the complement is $16384$, which is exactly one quarter. The figure is not an artefact of
the numbers chosen: it is $\frac{1}{4}$ for any even word length, and getting close to it for
any word length at all.

What makes this dangerous in a control system is the absence of any signal. There is no
exception, no overflow flag that the high-level code checks, and no value that looks wrong. The
program compares $-106$ with zero, correctly concludes that $-106 < 0$, and proceeds. The only
way to find the bug is to reason about the range of the operands, which is exactly what the
question asks for.

The fix in part (d) is worth dwelling on because it is not the obvious one. The obvious fix is
to widen the integer, and that works — nine bits are always enough for the difference of two
eight-bit numbers. But it costs memory in exactly the applications where eight-bit
representation was chosen for compactness, and it is not needed. The sign test costs two
comparisons and removes the problem entirely, because the dangerous case is precisely the case
where the signs differ, and in that case the answer is known without subtracting anything.

More generally, this is the reason comparisons in serious code are written as comparisons
rather than as subtractions. A compiler may or may not be able to prove that a subtraction is
safe; a sign test is safe by construction, and "safe by construction" is worth more than "safe
because the inputs happen to be small".

provenance.resource_origin: AP Computer Science A items on the range of primitive integer types and on overflow, typically asking what value results when an int exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE.
provenance.adaptation: The source asks what value is produced by an overflow, so the candidate observes the symptom and stops. Here the overflow is embedded in a comparison, which is how it actually appears in code, and the candidate must establish the range over which the comparison is trustworthy before counting the failures. Part (c) turns the symptom into an exact failure rate over the whole input space — a combinatorial count the source never asks for — and part (d) asks for a fix that does not require widening the type. Context, structure, given-versus-asked and the reasoning chain all differ.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Treat the comparison as ordinary arithmetic, assume that a subtraction of two representable integers is itself representable, and conclude that the line is correct.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The difference of two eight-bit values needs nine bits, so the subtraction wraps whenever $|a - b| > 127$; the wrap adds or subtracts $256$, which is larger than the representable magnitude and therefore reverses the sign rather than merely perturbing it.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The line reports that $100$ is below $-50$, and it does so for exactly a quarter of all ordered pairs of readings — $16384$ of the $65536$ — with no run-time indication that anything failed.

solution_skeleton: Compute the true difference and reduce it modulo 256 into the representable range
Identify the interval of differences for which no wrap occurs
Count the ordered pairs giving each difference as 256 minus the absolute difference
Sum over the correct interval and subtract from the total number of pairs
Compare signs first so that the subtraction is only performed when it cannot overflow
verification.method: Every count is reproduced by direct summation over the range $-255 \le d \le 255$; the proportion is checked to be exactly $0.25$, and the same-sign bound $|a-b| \le 127$ is verified at the extremes of the representable range.
assertions: sum([256-abs(d) for d in range(-255,-128)]) + sum([256-abs(d) for d in range(128,256)]) == 16384

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.syllabus_ref: B2.4 Programming algorithms (analysis of algorithms; efficiency of an algorithm)
questions.subtopic: B2.4 A nested loop whose inner trip count depends on the outer index
questions.challenge_mechanism: Two nested loops over the same range look like $O(N^{2})$ and are not, because the inner loop does not run $N$ times — it runs $\lfloor N/I \rfloor$ times, where $I$ is the outer index. The total is the summatory divisor function, which grows as $N\ln N$ rather than $N^{2}$: at $N = 1000$ the true count is $7069$ against the $500000$ a quadratic estimate would predict, a factor of about seventy.
questions.question:
A programmer writes the following routine to count the divisors of every integer up to
$N$.

```
COUNT = 0
for I = 1 to N
    for J = I to N step I
        COUNT = COUNT + 1
    next J
next I
output COUNT
```

(a) Trace the routine for $N = 6$ and state the value output. \tag{4}

(b) Show that the number of times the inner loop body executes is

$$\sum_{I=1}^{N} \left\lfloor \frac{N}{I} \right\rfloor . \tag{4}$$

(c) Determine the value output when $N = 1000$, and hence determine the ratio of the number of
iterations to $N^{2}$. \tag{5}

(d) Explain why the time complexity of the routine is $\mathrm{O}(N \log N)$ rather than
$\mathrm{O}(N^{2})$. \tag{3}

parts.label: a
parts.text: Trace the routine for $N = 6$ and state the value output.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the number of inner-loop executions is the sum from I = 1 to N of the floor of N divided by I.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the value output when $N = 1000$, and hence determine the ratio of the number of iterations to $N$ squared.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the time complexity is O(N log N) rather than O(N squared).

questions.answer:
(a) Tracing the outer loop (M1):

| $I$ | values taken by $J$ | inner iterations |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 | 6 |
| 2 | 2, 4, 6 | 3 |
| 3 | 3, 6 | 2 |
| 4 | 4 | 1 |
| 5 | 5 | 1 |
| 6 | 6 | 1 |

The inner counts are $6, 3, 2, 1, 1, 1$ (A1) and the total is $6 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 14$
(A1). So the routine outputs $14$ (A1). Note that only the first of the six passes runs the
full $N$ times; by the fourth pass the inner loop executes once.

(b) On the pass with outer index $I$, the inner variable $J$ takes the values
$I, 2I, 3I, \ldots$ up to $N$ (M1). The largest multiple of $I$ not exceeding $N$ is
$\left\lfloor \frac{N}{I} \right\rfloor \cdot I$ (A1), so the number of values taken is exactly
$\left\lfloor \frac{N}{I} \right\rfloor$ (A1). Summing over the $N$ passes of the outer loop
gives the stated expression (AG).

(c) Evaluating the sum for $N = 1000$ (M1):

$$\sum_{I=1}^{1000} \left\lfloor \frac{1000}{I} \right\rfloor = 7069 \tag{A1}$$

The ratio to $N^{2}$ is (M1)

$$\frac{7069}{1000^{2}} = \frac{7069}{1000000} = 0.00707 \tag{A1}$$

so the routine performs about $0.7\%$ of the iterations a quadratic algorithm would. Equally
tellings is the comparison with $N\ln N$:

$$N\ln N = 1000 \times 6.908 = 6908 \qquad \frac{7069}{6908} = 1.02 \tag{A1}$$

so the actual count is within about $2\%$ of $N\ln N$. A candidate who assumed $\mathrm{O}(N^{2})$
would predict roughly half a million iterations and would be wrong by a factor of about
seventy.

(d) From (b), the iteration count is $\sum_{I=1}^{N} \left\lfloor \frac{N}{I} \right\rfloor
\le \sum_{I=1}^{N} \frac{N}{I} = N \sum_{I=1}^{N} \frac{1}{I}$ (M1). The sum on the right is
the $N$th harmonic number, $H_{N}$, which satisfies $\ln(N+1) \le H_{N} \le 1 + \ln N$ and is
therefore $\mathrm{O}(\log N)$ (A1). It follows that the whole expression is
$\mathrm{O}(N\log N)$ (AG). The bound is tight rather than merely an upper limit, as the
numerical comparison in (c) shows: at $N = 1000$ the actual count of $7069$ sits about $2\%$
above $N\ln N = 6908$, and the gap between the two is the linear term that the floors and the
Euler–Mascheroni constant contribute.

It is worth being explicit about what the bound does and does not say. Replacing the floor by
$\frac{N}{I}$ can only increase the total, so the argument gives a genuine upper bound on the
running time and never an underestimate; and since the harmonic sum is also $\Omega(\log N)$,
the estimate is of the right order and not merely safe. What the argument does not do is give
a constant: $\mathrm{O}(N\log N)$ says nothing about whether the constant is $1$ or $100$, and
for small $N$ the constant can matter more than the growth rate. The numerical work in (c) is
what supplies the constant, which is why both parts are needed.

One further observation, for a candidate who wants to check the result independently: the sum
$\sum \lfloor N/I \rfloor$ counts the pairs $(I, J)$ with $I \mid J$ and $J \le N$, so it is
the total number of divisors possessed by all the integers from $1$ to $N$. It is therefore
also the number of times a naive divisor-counting routine would increment its counter, which
is exactly what the code in the stem is doing. Recognising that gives the answer a second
meaning and a second way to verify it.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for a systematic trace — a table, or an equivalent listing of the values taken by
$J$ for each $I$. (A1) for the inner counts $6, 3, 2, 1, 1, 1$. (A1) for the total $14$.
(A1) for the observation that only the first pass runs the full $N$ times; this is the
observation that drives the rest of the item and a bare answer of $14$ with no trace earns only
the first (A1).

(b) (M1) for identifying the values taken by $J$ as the multiples of $I$. (A1) for
$\left\lfloor \frac{N}{I} \right\rfloor \cdot I$ as the largest multiple. (A1) for the count.
(AG) for the summation. Allow a candidate who argues via $\lfloor (N-I)/I \rfloor + 1$ and
simplifies, but the simplification must be shown.

(c) (M1) for attempting the sum; accept a stated value obtained by computation, since summing
a thousand terms by hand is not the point. (A1) for $7069$. (M1) for dividing by $N^{2}$.
(A1) for $0.00707$. (A1) for the comparison with $N \ln N$ or with the quadratic estimate.
Accept the ratio as $0.0071$.

(d) (M1) for bounding the floor by $\frac{N}{I}$. (A1) for identifying the harmonic sum as
$\mathrm{O}(\log N)$. (AG) for the conclusion. A candidate who merely says "the inner loop does
not run $N$ times" earns the first (M1) only.

Note: do not accept an argument that the answer is $\mathrm{O}(N)$ — the harmonic sum is not
constant.
questions.explanation:
Nested loops are taught with a rule of thumb — multiply the trip counts — and the rule
of thumb is right often enough to become a reflex. It fails here because it assumes the inner
count is independent of the outer index, and here it is the outer index itself that sets it.

Once the count is written as $\sum \lfloor N/I \rfloor$, the growth rate is a known quantity.
The floors can only reduce the total, so bounding above by $N\sum \frac{1}{I}$ is legitimate,
and the harmonic sum is $\mathrm{O}(\log N)$. That gives $N \log N$ rather than $N^{2}$, and
the numerical check in part (c) confirms the bound is not merely an upper limit: $N \ln N$ at
$N = 1000$ is $6908$ against an actual count of $7069$, about $2\%$ apart.

The factor-of-seventy gap between $7069$ and the half-million a quadratic estimate predicts is
the practical reason this matters. A programmer who believes the routine is quadratic will
refuse to run it at $N = 1000$ and will rewrite it unnecessarily; one who recognises
$N \log N$ will not. The difference between the two growth rates only widens with $N$: at
$N = 10^{6}$ the true count is about $1.4 \times 10^{7}$ against $10^{12}$ for a genuinely
quadratic routine.

There is also a substantive point hiding in the trace. The routine looks like it might be
counting something more exotic than it is, but $\sum \lfloor N/I \rfloor$ counts the number of
pairs $(I, J)$ with $I \mid J$ and $J \le N$ — that is, the total number of divisors possessed
by all the integers up to $N$. Recognising that gives the result a second, independent meaning,
and it is why the count grows the way it does: most integers have few divisors, and only the
small values of $I$ contribute many terms.

Finally, note that the floors matter for the exact value but not for the order of growth.
Dropping them changes the answer by at most $N$ out of roughly $N \ln N$, which is a lower-order
term — and knowing which simplifications change the answer and which do not is most of what
algorithm analysis consists of.

provenance.resource_origin: AP Computer Science A items presenting a short nested-loop code segment and asking how many times a statement executes, or which informal order of growth best describes the running time.
provenance.adaptation: The source's nested loops have inner bounds that are either constant or a fixed function of the outer bound such as $I$ or $N-I$, so the trip counts are triangular or quadratic and the rule of thumb works. Here the inner loop *steps* by $I$, which makes the count $\lfloor N/I \rfloor$ and the total the summatory divisor function — a quantity that looks quadratic and is $N \log N$. Part (c) asks for the exact value at $N = 1000$ and for the comparison against both $N^{2}$ and $N\ln N$, neither of which the source asks for, and part (d) requires the harmonic-series argument rather than an informal judgement. Context, structure, given-versus-asked and the reasoning chain all differ.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: See two nested loops each running up to $N$, multiply the trip counts, and conclude the routine is $\mathrm{O}(N^{2})$ with about $N^{2}$ iterations.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The inner loop steps by $I$, so on the pass with outer index $I$ it executes $\lfloor N/I \rfloor$ times rather than $N$ times; the total is a harmonic-weighted sum, and only the first pass runs anything like the full range.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: About $500\,000$ iterations for $N = 1000$ against the true $7069$ — an overestimate by a factor of roughly seventy, and enough to make a perfectly usable routine look as though it should be rewritten.

solution_skeleton: Trace the outer loop and list the values taken by the inner variable
Express the inner trip count as the floor of N divided by I
Sum the expression over the outer index
Evaluate the sum at N equals 1000 and compare with N squared and N log N
Bound the sum by N times the harmonic series to get the order of growth
verification.method: The trace for $N = 6$ and the sums for $N = 10$, $N = 100$ and $N = 1000$ are computed directly; the totals are compared with $N^{2}$ and with $N\ln N$.

figure.caption: The same $64\ \mathrm{kB}$ window sent at $100\ \mathrm{Mbps}$ and at $1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$, against the $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ round-trip time they share. The sender finishes transmitting long before the acknowledgement returns.

questions.challenge_mechanism: Doubling the link rate tenfold leaves the throughput unchanged, and the arithmetic that shows it is simple enough to be embarrassing. Throughput with a windowed protocol is window divided by round-trip time, and the link rate never appears in that expression once the window is smaller than the bandwidth-delay product. The data rate is a red herring, and the quantity that is actually binding — the window — is the one nothing in the stem draws attention to.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time to transmit one window at $100\ \mathrm{Mbps}$ and hence the maximum throughput achievable with this window.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the new transmission time for one window at $1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$ and the new maximum throughput.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the window size, in bytes, needed to make full use of the $1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$ link.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the upgrade produced no improvement, and state what should be changed.

questions.answer:
(a) One window is $65536 \times 8 = 524288$ bits (A1). At $100\ \mathrm{Mbps}$ the
transmission time is

$$t = \frac{524288}{1.00 \times 10^{8}} = 5.24\ \mathrm{ms} \tag{A1}$$

The sender must then wait for the acknowledgement, so one window is delivered per round-trip
time and the maximum throughput is

$$\frac{524288\ \mathrm{bits}}{0.040\ \mathrm{s}} = 1.31 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{bps}
= 13.1\ \mathrm{Mbps} \tag{A1}$$

Note that this is $13.1\%$ of the link rate, even though the sender is idle for
$40 - 5.24 = 34.8\ \mathrm{ms}$ of every $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ cycle.

(b) At $1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$ the transmission time falls by a factor of ten (A1):

$$t = \frac{524288}{1.00 \times 10^{9}} = 0.524\ \mathrm{ms} \tag{A1}$$

The throughput is unchanged, because the amount sent per round trip has not changed (A1):

$$\frac{524288}{0.040} = 13.1\ \mathrm{Mbps} \tag{A1}$$

The sender is now idle for $39.5\ \mathrm{ms}$ of every $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ — it finishes sooner
and then waits longer, and the two effects cancel exactly.

(c) To keep the link busy the window must be at least the bandwidth-delay product (M1):

$$W = B \times \mathrm{RTT} = 1.00 \times 10^{9} \times 0.040 = 4.0 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{bits}
\tag{A1}$$

$$W = \frac{4.0 \times 10^{7}}{8} = 5.0 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{bytes} = 5.0\ \mathrm{MB}
\tag{A1}$$

Compared with the existing window this is (A1)

$$\frac{5.0 \times 10^{6}}{65536} = 76.3$$

times larger (A1). Equivalently, the existing window keeps the link busy for
$\frac{5.24}{40} = 13.1\%$ of the cycle at $100\ \mathrm{Mbps}$ and for
$\frac{0.524}{40} = 1.31\%$ at $1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$, so the utilisation falls by a factor of ten
exactly as the rate rises by a factor of ten, and the two effects cancel precisely.

Two checks are worth applying to the answer. First, the required window scales with the
round-trip time as well as with the rate, so halving the latency would halve the window
needed — a reminder that latency and bandwidth are separate constraints and can be traded
against each other. Second, $5.0\ \mathrm{MB}$ of unacknowledged data is a large amount to have
in flight, and in practice the window would be limited by the receiving system's buffer and by
congestion control rather than by the arithmetic here; the bandwidth-delay product gives the
minimum window that makes the link usable, not a window that any real system would necessarily
grant.

(d) The upgrade improved the rate at which data is placed on the link but not the amount that
may be in flight (A1). With a windowed protocol the throughput is
$\frac{\text{window}}{\mathrm{RTT}}$ whenever the window is smaller than the bandwidth-delay
product, and the link rate does not appear in that expression at all (R1). The window here,
$64\ \mathrm{kB}$, is well below the $5.0\ \mathrm{MB}$ bandwidth-delay product of the upgraded
link, so the link is idle for $98.7\%$ of each cycle and the tenfold increase in rate is
invisible (A1).

What should be changed is the window, not the link (A1): the sending software needs a window of
about $5\ \mathrm{MB}$ to use the $1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$ link, and with the existing $64\ \mathrm{kB}$
window there was no point buying the upgrade at all. The general diagnostic is to compute the
bandwidth-delay product before paying for bandwidth; if the window is smaller, the money is
being spent on the wrong thing.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (A1) for converting the window to $524288$ bits. (A1) for $5.24\ \mathrm{ms}$.
(A1) for $13.1\ \mathrm{Mbps}$; accept $1.31 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{bps}$. A candidate who
divides the link rate by ten or otherwise tries to include the link rate in the throughput
earns at most the first (A1).

(b) (A1) for $0.524\ \mathrm{ms}$. (A1) for the observation that the window has not changed.
(A1) for $13.1\ \mathrm{Mbps}$. (A1) for the cancellation — the sender finishes sooner and waits
longer. A candidate who reports a higher throughput here has not understood windowing and loses
the last three marks.

(c) (M1) for the bandwidth-delay product. (A1) for $4.0 \times 10^{7}$ bits. (A1) for
$5.0 \times 10^{6}$ bytes. (A1) for the ratio $76.3$. (A1) for the utilisation argument.
Accept $5\ \mathrm{MB}$ or $4.77\ \mathrm{MiB}$ provided the unit is stated.

(d) (A1) for the distinction between the rate and the amount in flight. (R1) for the
throughput expression, which must be stated as window over round-trip time. (A1) for the
quantitative comparison with the bandwidth-delay product. (A1) for identifying the window as
what should change.

Condonation: allow a candidate who says "increase the window" without the figure, provided the
reasoning about the amount in flight is present.
questions.explanation:
The result is counter-intuitive enough that it is worth stating in one sentence: with a
windowed protocol, throughput is the amount you may have in flight divided by the time a
round trip takes, and the speed of the link does not appear in that expression at all until the
window exceeds the bandwidth-delay product.

The arithmetic makes it concrete. At $100\ \mathrm{Mbps}$ the $64\ \mathrm{kB}$ window takes
$5.24\ \mathrm{ms}$ to put on the wire, and then the sender sits idle for the remaining
$34.8\ \mathrm{ms}$ of the round trip. It is using the link $13.1\%$ of the time. Upgrade to
$1\ \mathrm{Gbps}$ and the same window takes $0.524\ \mathrm{ms}$ — the sender finishes sooner
and waits longer, and since the amount delivered per round trip has not changed, neither has the
throughput. Utilisation drops to $1.31\%$. The tenfold improvement in rate is exactly cancelled
by a tenfold drop in utilisation.

This is why the bandwidth-delay product is the first thing to compute. It is the amount of data
that must be in flight to keep the pipe full: rate times round-trip time. For the upgraded link
that is $1\ \mathrm{Gbps} \times 40\ \mathrm{ms} = 5.0\ \mathrm{MB}$, which is $76$ times the
window the software actually uses. Until the window is increased — in the protocol
configuration, not in the hardware — the upgrade buys nothing.

The practical lesson generalises well past this question. Latency and bandwidth are different
constraints and they bind at different times: if the window is small, latency binds and
bandwidth is irrelevant; if the window is large enough, bandwidth binds and latency stops
mattering. Buying more of the one that is not binding is the commonest way to spend money on a
network and get nothing for it, and the way to tell which one is binding is to compare the
window with the bandwidth-delay product.

The figure is there to make the idle time visible. Both rows show the same $64\ \mathrm{kB}$, and
what changes between them is only how much of the $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ is coloured in.

provenance.inspired_by: UK A-Level Computer Science: bandwidth, latency and the factors affecting data transmission rates
provenance.resource_origin: UK A-Level Computer Science items on network performance, typically asking students to calculate a file transfer time from a file size and a stated bandwidth, or to explain the difference between bandwidth and latency.
provenance.adaptation: The source's transfer-time questions give a file size and a rate and ask for the time, so bandwidth is always the governing quantity and latency never enters. Here a sliding window is introduced, which makes the amount in flight the binding constraint and reduces the link rate to a quantity that cancels out. Parts (a) and (b) ask for the throughput at two rates tenfold apart and the answer is identical, which the source's framing can never produce, and part (c) asks for the bandwidth-delay product. Context, structure, given-versus-asked and the reasoning chain all differ.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Recompute the throughput using the new, higher link rate, on the assumption that a faster link transfers the same data faster.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The amount of data allowed in flight is fixed at $64\ \mathrm{kB}$ by the window, so throughput is window over round-trip time; raising the rate only makes the sender finish sooner and then idle for longer.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: A predicted tenfold increase in throughput that does not occur; the true throughput is $13.1\ \mathrm{Mbps}$ at both rates, and the upgrade is worth nothing until the window grows by a factor of about $76$.

solution_skeleton: Convert the window from bytes to bits
Divide by the link rate to get the transmission time
Divide the window by the round-trip time to get the throughput
Multiply the new rate by the round-trip time to get the required window
Compare the required window with the one in use
verification.method: Transmission times and throughputs are evaluated at both rates; the required window is computed as rate times round-trip time and compared with $65536$ bytes; utilisation is computed as the ratio of transmission time to round-trip time at each rate.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.syllabus_ref: A4.2 Data preprocessing (HL only) (normalisation, standardisation, outlier handling)
questions.subtopic: A4.2 Choosing a scaling method when one outlier dominates the range
questions.challenge_mechanism: Both scaling methods are legitimate and they disagree by a factor of more than three in how well they separate the typical readings. Min-max puts the outlier at $1.0$ and squeezes the nine ordinary values into the bottom $8.9\%$ of the interval; standardisation spreads them over $3.5$ times as much of the range. The choice is a judgement, but it is a judgement that can be made quantitative: compare the scaled gap between consecutive typical values.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the standard deviation of the ten values as recorded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the min-max scaled values of 10, 18 and 1400, and calculate the scaled gap between consecutive typical values.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the standardised values of 10, 18 and 1400, calculate the corresponding scaled gap, and compare the two methods.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Hence explain which scaling method the team should prefer for this data set.

questions.answer:
(a) The nine typical values are the integers $10$ to $18$, whose sum is
$\frac{9(10 + 18)}{2} = 126$; adding $1400$ gives $1526$ and the mean is

$$\bar{x} = \frac{1526}{10} = 152.6 \tag{A1}$$

Note that the mean already sits far above every genuine reading: the true centre of the nine
typical values is $14$, and the single error has moved it by $138.6$.

The sum of squared deviations is most safely found from
$\sum x^{2} - n\bar{x}^{2}$ (M1). Here

$$\sum x^{2} = 100 + 121 + \cdots + 324 + 1960000 = 1824 + 1960000 = 1961824$$

and $n\bar{x}^{2} = 10 \times 152.6^{2} = 10 \times 23286.76 = 232867.6$, so

$$\sum (x - \bar{x})^{2} = 1961824 - 232867.6 = 1728956.4 \tag{A1}$$

The outlier contributes $1247.4^{2} = 1556006.8$ of that, which is $90.0\%$ of the whole
total. The population variance is $\frac{1728956.4}{10} = 172895.6$ and

$$\sigma = \sqrt{172895.6} = 415.8 \tag{A1}$$

(b) Min–max scaling maps $x$ to $\frac{x - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}$, and here
$x_{\min} = 10$ and $x_{\max} = 1400$, so the divisor is $1390$ (M1):

$$\frac{10 - 10}{1390} = 0.000, \qquad \frac{18 - 10}{1390} = 0.00576, \qquad
\frac{1400 - 10}{1390} = 1.000 \tag{A1}$$

The typical values therefore occupy the interval $[0,\ 0.00576]$ — the bottom $0.58\%$ of the
range — and the outlier sits alone at $1.000$ (A1). The scaled gap between consecutive typical
values, which are one minute apart in the original data, is

$$\frac{1}{1390} = 0.000719 \tag{A1}$$

(c) Standardising maps $x$ to $\frac{x - \bar{x}}{\sigma}$ (M1):

$$\frac{10 - 152.6}{415.8} = -0.343, \qquad \frac{18 - 152.6}{415.8} = -0.324, \qquad
\frac{1400 - 152.6}{415.8} = 3.00 \tag{A1}$$

The typical values occupy $[-0.343,\ -0.324]$ and the outlier sits at $3.00$ (A1). The scaled
gap between consecutive typical values is

$$\frac{1}{415.8} = 0.00241 \tag{A1}$$

which is $\frac{0.00241}{0.000719} = 3.34$ times the min–max gap (A1). Standardisation
therefore preserves about three and a third times as much resolution among the typical readings
as min–max does, even though it is far from ideal: the outlier still inflates $\sigma$ from
about $2.4$ to $415.8$ and drags the mean to $152.6$, more than ten times the largest genuine
reading. Note also that $3.00$ is the largest z-score any value in a data set of ten can have,
so the outlier is pressing against the ceiling that the sample size allows.

(d) Neither method should be used on the raw data (A1). The right first step is to correct or
remove the erroneous $1400$, since it is a known data-entry fault rather than a genuine
observation; with it removed the range is $8$, the mean is $14$ and the choice of scaler barely
matters (A1). If the value must be retained, standardisation is preferable to min–max because
the mean and standard deviation are less sensitive to a single extreme value than the minimum
and maximum are — the outlier moves $\sigma$ but does not set it, whereas it sets $x_{\max}$
directly (A1). Better still is a robust scaler based on the median and interquartile range,
which for this data gives a scaled gap of $\frac{1}{5} = 0.2$, about $278$ times the min–max
resolution.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (A1) for the sum or the mean $152.6$. (M1) for setting up the sum of squared
deviations. (A1) for the outlier's squared deviation $1556006.76$. (A1) for
$\sigma = 415.8$; accept $[415, 416]$. Allow the sample standard deviation ($s = 438.3$)
provided it is identified as such, with full marks.

(b) (M1) for the divisor $1390$. (A1) for the three scaled values. (A1) for identifying that
the typical values fall in the bottom fraction of the range. (A1) for the gap $0.000719$.

(c) (M1) for the standardisation formula. (A1) for the three z-scores. (A1) for the interval
occupied by the typical values. (A1) for the gap $0.00241$. (A1) for the ratio $3.34$.

Forfeiture: a candidate who uses the *cleaned* mean or standard deviation in (c) has answered a
different question and earns at most the first (M1) — the item is explicitly about what happens
before cleaning.

(d) (A1) for recommending cleaning first. (A1) for the consequence of cleaning. (A1) for
comparing the sensitivity of the two scalers, or for proposing a robust alternative with the
figure $0.2$.

Note: a candidate who simply states that min–max is "affected by outliers" has not used the
quantitative work from (b) and (c) and earns at most one mark.
questions.explanation:
Min–max scaling has a single point of failure: it is defined by the two most extreme
values in the data set. If one of those is wrong, the whole scaling is wrong, and it is wrong in
a way that is easy to miss because the output still looks like a properly scaled feature —
values in $[0, 1]$, outlier at the top, everything else near the bottom. Nothing announces the
problem.

Quantifying the damage is what makes the choice a decision rather than an opinion. Consecutive
typical readings are one minute apart, and after min–max scaling they sit $0.000719$ apart. For
a distance-based algorithm such as k-means, that is very close to indistinguishable: the
distances between ordinary points have been compressed by a factor of $1390$ relative to what
they were, while the distance to the outlier has been set to the maximum the scale allows.

Standardisation does better, and the reason is structural. It is defined by the mean and the
standard deviation, which are computed from every value, so a single extreme reading shifts them
without determining them. Here the outlier is worth $3.0\sigma$ — large, but finite, and it
does not set the scale. The resolution improves by a factor of about $3.3$. That is a real
improvement, but it should not be oversold: the outlier has inflated $\sigma$ from roughly
$2.4$ to $415.8$, so standardisation is compromised too, just less catastrophically.

The honest answer to (d) is that both are the wrong question. The value $1400$ is a known
decimal-point error; there is no statistical method that is the right response to a typo. Clean
it, and with the remaining nine values the range is $8$, the standard deviation is about $2.4$,
and the choice between scalers has almost no effect on the model. Where cleaning is not
possible — because the extreme value might be genuine — a robust scaler based on the median and
interquartile range gives a resolution of $0.2$ here, roughly $278$ times what min–max
delivers.

The more general lesson is that preprocessing choices are not neutral. Two defensible scalings
of the same feature can put the ordinary values $0.0007$ apart or $0.2$ apart, and a
distance-based model will behave completely differently in the two cases. Measuring the
resolution, rather than asserting that one method is "better", is what turns that choice into
something a data scientist can defend.

provenance.inspired_by: AP Computer Science Principles / AP Statistics: data cleaning, outliers and the effect on summary statistics
provenance.resource_origin: AP-level items on the effect of an outlier on the mean, range and standard deviation, and introductory machine-learning material presenting min-max normalisation and z-score standardisation as alternative preprocessing steps.
provenance.adaptation: The two traditions are separate in the source: statistics items ask how an outlier moves the mean, and ML material lists the two scalers without comparing them. Here they are combined into a single quantitative comparison, with the resolution — the scaled gap between consecutive typical values — as the measure, which neither source defines. The outlier is given a specific physical cause (a lost decimal point) so that part (d) can ask whether scaling is the right response at all, and a robust alternative is quantified alongside. Context, structure, given-versus-asked and the reasoning chain all differ.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Pick a scaler from the standard list and apply it, noting that min–max is generally described as sensitive to outliers without checking how much difference that makes here.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: Min–max is defined by the extreme values themselves, so the single erroneous reading sets the whole scale and compresses the nine genuine readings into the bottom $0.58\%$ of the interval.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: A scaled separation of $0.000719$ between consecutive typical readings under min–max, against $0.00253$ under standardisation and $0.2$ under a robust scaler — the same data, separated by a factor of nearly three hundred depending on a choice made without looking.

solution_skeleton: Sum the ten values and divide by ten for the mean
Accumulate the squared deviations and take the square root for the standard deviation
Scale by the observed range for min-max and read off the gap
Scale by the mean and standard deviation for the z-score and read off the gap
Compare the two gaps and note the robust alternative based on the interquartile range
verification.method: The mean, the sum of squared deviations and the standard deviation are recomputed; both scalings are applied to the smallest, largest typical and outlying values, and the two resolutions are compared against the robust interquartile resolution.
